# Systems Architecture and Performance {#sec-optimization}

This section describes the storage and execution machinery that keeps the v5
engine realtime at hundreds of thousands of stored turns. It covers only
surviving architecture. The full optimization ledger, including
micro-optimizations and proof traces for subsystems the 2026-10 ablation later
removed, is preserved verbatim in Appendix E
(`docs/paper/appendix/optimization_ledger.qmd`).

The design rule throughout is that SQLite stays authoritative. Every resident
structure below is a cache or index that can be rebuilt from SQLite, and
retrieval results are byte-identical whether a structure is warm or rebuilt.
None of these structures branches on `source_id` or modality.

## Content-Addressed Embedding Arena

Several in-memory consumers hold the same stored vectors: the processor
retrieval surface, the historical and current supersession and seed surfaces,
rollback snapshots and borrowed supersession candidates. Before the arena each
kept its own copy. Now one process-wide arena holds each vector once, as an
immutable, reference-counted float32 row, and every consumer holds an 8-byte
handle.

* **Content addressing.** Rows are keyed by their exact bits. Stored embedding
  rows are append-only in SQLite (inserted and deleted, never updated), so
  equal bits always mean the same vector and sharing is exact.
* **Copy-on-write.** A new representation of a memory is a new row. A rollback
  snapshot copies handles, not vectors.
* **Layout.** Rows sit in 64-byte-aligned chunks that never move. Exact scans
  read rows in place and evaluate the same per-row Eigen expressions as the
  flat buffers they replaced, so ranking is bit-identical.
* **Family collapse.** The cosine-family index keeps only a side table of block
  norms per historical entry and re-expands the normalized vector from the row
  on use.

Together with the in-memory route below, the arena cut route search at 111k
turns from 16.4/24.8 ms to 3.8/4.6 ms (p50/p95) and peak RSS by 614 MB, with
packets byte-identical (PR #28).

## Rollback Journal

`Process()` and `Flush()` must restore exact processor state when their SQLite
transaction fails, and an Ephemeral query must leave no trace. A naive full
context snapshot copied every open accumulator and working-memory record on
each signal. That made a long Natural unit of `U` signals cost `O(U^2)` record
copies in total.

The engine journals ownership instead:

* An ordinary non-boundary signal records only the original vector lengths of
  the active source, then appends in place: amortized `O(1)`.
* A path that may mutate or clear prior records (accepted storage, accumulator
  reset after a flush, or an accepted interrupt reset) takes one deep backup of
  the active source first, so that transition copies `O(U)` once.
* Working-memory appends roll back by original length. An evicted slot's
  record vectors move into the journal instead of being copied.
* Success discards the journal. Failure restores ownership or the backup.

A caller-supplied `IOperation` root keeps the automatic full-context snapshot,
so hookless custom operations still roll back exactly. The private production
root is the only one whose mutation sites carry the journal contract.

## Sparse Route and In-Memory Route

Above a knob-derived population, dense seeding does not scan every vector.
It walks a sparse, persisted HNSW-style route [@malkov2018efficient] over the
current long-term surface. Its capacities are functions of the knobs. With
$F$, $S$ and $T$ clamped to $[0,1]$:

$$
C = \operatorname{round}(256 + 256F + 128S + 128T),\quad
B = \operatorname{round}(64 + 64F + 32S + 32T),\quad
A = 2C + 2B.
$$

At neutral knobs $C = 512$, $B = 128$ and $A = 1{,}280$. A query inspects at
most $8C$ to $9C$ canonical rows (the floor resets on each recenter and the
ceiling rises by $R = \max(2, \lfloor B/16 \rfloor)$ per query), plus at most
$A$ rows from the consolidation snapshot. Every routed row is reranked by
exact cosine, and at most $A$ identities go on to eligibility, family collapse
and final scoring. If eligibility or family collapse leaves the proposal short
of the requested seed count, the route discards it and the exact SQL seed path
runs instead. A short result is never returned as complete.

* **Epochs.** New memories join a dirty journal in the writing transaction.
  `Consolidate()` seals at most $C$ dirty identities into the route and
  recenters its activation snapshot on the active-signal ring centroid. That is
  all maintenance does now (@sec-consolidation). The engine recommends a pass
  once $C$ memories have been written since the last one, and requires one at
  $C \times$ `ConsolidationEscalationMultiplier(T)`. This restored 44
  consolidations on BEAM-10M conversation 7 after retrieval competition, the
  previous hint source, was removed.
* **Admission.** A full neighbour list admits a closer node by replacing a
  member, but never a member for which that link is its only level-0 inbound
  link. Distance-only replacement had left 1.5% of nodes with no inbound link
  and 2.9% unreachable at 443k nodes. After the fix, 98.99% of nodes are
  reachable and none lacks an inbound link (PR #28).
* **In-memory route.** Opening the route loads its generation's node rows once,
  in 4,096-row chunks, into a resident graph whose nodes hold adjacency and an
  arena handle. Traversal never reads SQLite, and each committed seal replaces
  exactly the rows it wrote. The resident graph mirrors the persisted route; it
  is not a second write path.
* **Supersession reuse.** Above the cutover, write-time supersession search
  reuses the route instead of scanning history. Historical rows visited per
  turn on BEAM conversation 7 fell from up to 43k to 0, and the written edges
  are approximate (Jaccard 0.985 against the exact scan).

The round-3 ablation kept the route on cost alone (@sec-experimental). At
111,527 chained turns, switching it off raised instructions by 26%, ingest
past 100k turns from 95 to 170 ms per turn, query median from 33 to 45 ms and
RSS from 6.7 to 7.4 GB. The route is approximate, though: with it off, packet
gold-turn recall was 0.076 against 0.062 with it on, and judged sufficiency
moved +0.020 ± 0.052.

## WAL Checkpointer Thread

Each file-backed SQLite store owns a background checkpointer: its own
connection and thread. It runs PASSIVE checkpoints when the WAL reaches the
auto-checkpoint size (1,000 pages) and after every `Flush()`. Commits only
request a checkpoint.

* `Flush()` returns once its transaction is in the WAL, which is durable
  against a process crash. The background checkpoint then syncs it against
  power loss.
* Durable retention's post-commit barrier is one fsync of the WAL holding its
  commit, instead of a TRUNCATE checkpoint.
* Writes take the lock at `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, so `busy_timeout` covers every
  signal. This removed "database is locked" errors under ingest plus
  concurrent Ephemeral probes.

Under synthetic disk pressure (8 writers, 256 MB each with `F_FULLFSYNC`), a
foreground `Flush()` checkpoint stalled 99 to 161 ms. With the checkpointer,
`Flush()` took at most 5 ms (@sec-implementation). Under the I/O-pressure test
in PR #28, maximum consolidation time fell from 728 to 103 ms and maximum
`Flush()` time from 696 to 89 ms.

## Family-Collapse Bounds

Before the seed cap, near-duplicate embedding families collapse to one
representative (@sec-math). Comparing every candidate with every
representative would be quadratic, so each pair passes through sound filters
before any exact cosine:

1. **Partial squared distance.** Coordinate differences accumulate in
   16-coordinate vectorized blocks. A pair is rejected as soon as a completed
   block exceeds the squared-distance limit implied by the cosine threshold.
   Every omitted term is nonnegative, so this never rejects a true duplicate.
2. **Cauchy–Schwarz block bounds in two bases.** Coordinates are split into 32
   blocks. For normalized $x$ and $y$, $\cos(x, y) \le \sum_b \|x_b\| \|y_b\|$.
   The bound is computed both in the stored basis and in a normalized
   Walsh–Hadamard basis $H$, using $\cos(x,y) = \cos(Hx, Hy)$. Vectors that are
   sparse in coordinates are dense after $H$ and vice versa, so one of the two
   bounds is tight for both kinds of surface.
3. **Exact cosine** for the survivors.

Both bounds are upper bounds, so neither can exclude a pair that meets the
threshold. The normalized vector and both block-norm summaries are immutable
functions of an embedding, computed on first use and cached with the surface
entry. One event may run at most $2C$ exact checks. Once that budget is spent,
the remaining candidates are admitted rather than compared, which keeps the
work bounded at the cost of an occasional duplicate in the seed set. A
256-vector orthogonal-basis regression requires exact comparisons to stay
below a quarter of the all-pairs count.

## FTS5 Top-k Collector

The keyword channel (@sec-retrieval) runs BM25 over a contentless FTS5 index.
Two changes keep it bounded on large stores.

* **Document-frequency cut.** Query words whose index term occurs in more than
  $\max(64, 0.05N)$ of $N$ memories are dropped before the query runs. Their
  posting lists dominated query time but carry little BM25 weight. On a
  22.6k-turn store, FTS5 time per query fell from about 14 ms to 2 ms. The df
  probe itself stops at the cut.
* **Top-k collector.** FTS5's `ORDER BY rank` scores every matching row with
  `bm25()`, one document-size read each, and sorts them all. One six-word
  question matched 32.8k rows: 2 ms to match and 42 ms to rank. The engine
  registers an FTS5 auxiliary function, `cortext_bm25_topk`, that computes the
  same score term for term and keeps the best $2 \times 20 + 4$ rows in a heap.
  The over-fetch covers hits that later fail seed eligibility. It also skips
  the document-size read and the score of a row whose upper bound cannot
  enter the heap. At 443k turns, query CPU fell from 57.9/100.9 ms to
  24.6/37.6 ms (p50/p95) (PR #28).

## Resident Surfaces

Query-time channels read from resident structures that advance incrementally
instead of reloading.

| Surface | Contents | Maintenance |
|---|---|---|
| retrieval surface | current long-term vector and metadata per memory | kept across read-only queries and across `Flush()`, not reloaded; loaded as a stream at open |
| member index | int8 codes (dimension + 4 bytes) of the member signals of multi-signal long-term memories | reads signal ids above its mark; a WAL store starts a warm read on its own connection and thread at open, and the first query adopts it |
| cross-modal populations | one aligned matrix per stored modality of long-term signal vectors | loaded on first use by a query of another modality; then reads only rows above a long-term mark |
| standing set | at most 256 directive signals with their word stems | maintained in the writing transaction |
| sparse route | resident node graph of the published generation | replaced row-for-row by each committed seal |

What these surfaces bought, by the stage measurements in PR #28 and @sec-implementation:

* Keeping the retrieval surface across queries took the query median at 20k
  turns from 690 ms to 14.9 ms.
* Streaming the surface at open took 443k-turn reopen RSS from 6.77 to 4.57 GB.
* Resident cross-modal populations took queries over 125k image vectors from
  204/243 ms to 20/26 ms.
* Reading the member index at open, and advancing it past non-member rows,
  took 443k-turn queries from 400 ms to 30.7/44.5 ms p50/p95. The first query after open at
  BEAM-10M takes 26 ms instead of 54 ms.

The late-interaction codes are not resident. A query reads them for its top 64
candidates only, by one indexed statement.

## Remaining Costs

The engine is not flat in store size, and this section does not claim it is.

* sqlite-vec is a brute-force scan. Below the sparse cutover, and on every
  route fallback, exact seeding is linear in the current surface.
* Write-time supersession verification can still do history-sized work below
  the cutover, or when the route is unpublished or invalid.
* Opening a store is $O(\text{generation})$. It materializes the current
  surface and the resident route.
* Hydration cost follows the packet: contiguity, supersession attachments and
  evidence fitting are bounded per anchor, but payload reads scale with the
  bytes returned.

Further asymptotic gains need a change to candidate semantics, a storage or
index backend change, or a tiering policy. A tiering policy is a forgetting
policy, and @sec-negative shows how badly an unmeasured one fails.
